questions.stem: In dense fog your radar shows a vessel steady on your port bow at 3 miles. You cannot see her. A watchkeeper says, 'She is on our port side, so under the crossing rule we are the stand-on vessel.' What is the correct response?
options: He is right: with the contact on your port side you are stand-on under Rule 15 and must hold course and speed
Rule 19: no stand-on; act early, avoid a port turn
She is give-way because she is the one on your port side, so you can ignore her
Rule 19 makes the faster vessel stand-on
questions.explanation: A radar contact alone is not 'in sight', so Section II (Rules 11 to 18) does not apply; Rule 19 does. Rule 19 creates no stand-on vessel: every vessel that detects risk acts, and the guidance for a contact forward of the beam is to avoid turning to port (unless overtaking). Rule 15 needs vessels in sight, and no rule hands stand-on status to the faster vessel.

questions.stem: A 9 m yacht has her mainsail up and her engine running in forward gear at night. Which statement is correct?
options: She is a sailing vessel because her sails are up, and shows sidelights and a sternlight only
She is a sailing vessel and power-driven vessels must keep out of her way under Rule 18
She is a power-driven vessel and shows power-driven lights; Rule 12 does not apply to her
She is a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre
questions.explanation: A sailing vessel is one under sail provided any propelling machinery is not being used. With the engine in use she is power-driven, shows power-driven lights at night, and does not get sailing-vessel rights. Using the engine does not make her restricted in her ability to manoeuvre.

questions.stem: A sailing yacht on starboard tack is coming up from astern on a slow power-driven tug, bearing 170 degrees relative from the tug. The yacht's skipper says that a sailing vessel always has right of way over a power-driven vessel. Who keeps out of the way?
options: The tug, because Rule 18 requires power-driven vessels to give way to sailing vessels
The tug, because the yacht is on starboard tack
Neither: both must alter to starboard
The yacht, because Rule 13 on overtaking overrides Rule 18
questions.explanation: Rule 18 applies except where Rules 9, 10 and 13 otherwise require. A vessel more than 22.5 degrees abaft the other's beam is overtaking and keeps clear, whatever type she is. Tack matters only between two sailing vessels under Rule 12, and head-on action has no place when one vessel is overtaking.

questions.stem: Which pair of statements is correct for two power-driven vessels?
options: Head-on: both alter to starboard. Crossing: one with other to starboard gives way
Head-on: the vessel on the other's port side gives way. Crossing: both alter to starboard.
Head-on: both alter to port. Crossing: the vessel with the other on her own port side gives way.
Head-on: the larger vessel stands on. Crossing: the vessel with the other on her own starboard side stands on.
questions.explanation: In a head-on situation each vessel alters to starboard so they pass port to port, and neither is stand-on. In a crossing situation the vessel that has the other on her own starboard side keeps out of the way (and avoids crossing ahead if she can). Size does not decide either case, and altering to port in a head-on meeting is the classic mistake.

questions.stem: You are the stand-on vessel in a crossing situation with the give-way vessel on your port side. She has made no change and the distance is closing, but collision is not yet unavoidable by her action alone. Which statement is correct?
options: You must keep course and speed until collision is certain; any earlier action is forbidden
You may act, but avoid a port turn; five short if in doubt
You may turn to port to go round under her stern
You must act only after she sounds five short blasts
questions.explanation: Rule 17 has stages: keep course and speed; may act once it is apparent the give-way vessel is not acting appropriately; must act when she is so close that collision cannot be avoided by the give-way vessel alone. At stage 2 a power-driven stand-on vessel avoids a turn to port for a vessel on her own port side, and a vessel in doubt sounds at least five short and rapid blasts. The doubt signal is yours to give; you do not wait for hers.

questions.stem: A power-driven vessel is underway in open water and a small boat towing a single trolling line, with no fishing signals, is crossing from the power-driven vessel's port bow. Which statement is correct?
options: The power-driven vessel must give way, because every fishing vessel has priority under Rule 18
The power-driven vessel must give way because trolling boats are restricted in their ability to manoeuvre
Trolling isn't fishing; normal crossing rule, she keeps clear
Neither vessel is stand-on because the boat is fishing
questions.explanation: A vessel trolling, or fishing with gear that does not restrict her manoeuvrability, is not a vessel engaged in fishing, so Rule 18's priority for fishing vessels does not apply to her. Treated as an ordinary power-driven vessel with the other on her starboard side, she gives way under Rule 15. The other options assume a priority she does not have.

questions.stem: At night you see, at the masthead of an approaching vessel, an all-round white light above an all-round red light, together with sidelights and a sternlight. What is she?
options: A vessel fishing other than trawling, making way
A vessel trawling, making way
A vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre
A pilot vessel on pilotage duty, making way
questions.explanation: White over red at or near the masthead is a pilot vessel on pilotage duty; the sidelights and sternlight show she is making way. Red over white (the reverse) is fishing other than trawling, green over white is trawling, and red, white, red is restricted in ability to manoeuvre.

questions.stem: In thick fog you hear one prolonged blast followed by two short blasts, repeated about every 2 minutes, from a vessel you cannot see. Which statement is correct?
options: Any of NUC, RAM, CBD, sail, fishing or towing
She is altering course to port in the fog
She is a power-driven vessel making way
She is at anchor and warning you of her position
questions.explanation: One prolonged and two short every 2 minutes is the shared Rule 35 signal for several kinds of vessel, so it identifies a class but not the exact one. The manoeuvring signals (one short starboard, two short port, three short astern) are for vessels in sight, not for fog. A power-driven vessel making way sounds one prolonged, and an anchored vessel rings the bell.

questions.stem: A watchkeeper writes in the log after a near miss: 'We were stand-on, so the other vessel was fully to blame.' Which statement best reflects Rule 2?
options: Stand-on vessels cannot be held responsible for any collision at all
Stand-on is no full defence; neglect can still count
A departure from the Rules is allowed whenever the master thinks it sensible
Rule 2 binds give-way only
questions.explanation: Rule 2 says nothing excuses a vessel, owner, master or crew from the consequences of neglect, including neglecting sensible precautions. A departure from the Rules is justified only to avoid immediate danger. The Rule applies to every vessel.

questions.stem: At night in fog your radar shows nothing ahead. Later a large tow comes into view at close range, even though the radar bearing of a contact had been changing slowly. Which statement is correct?
options: A changing bearing always means there is no risk of collision
Radar shows every vessel, so the tow must have been hidden by AIS
Clear radar isn't clear water; risk can exist as bearing changes
Risk of collision exists only if the compass bearing is steady
questions.explanation: Radar can miss small vessels and floating objects, and AIS shows only vessels that transmit. A steady bearing means risk exists, but risk may exist even when the bearing changes, especially with a very large vessel, a tow, or any vessel at close range; if there is any doubt, risk is deemed to exist.
